abstract: |
  Infectious disease forecasting is useful for public health decision-making, including resource allocation and the timing of outbreak response interventions. Forecast quality is impacted by the quality of the data inputs, including spatio-temporal resolution, but the extent is still an area of active research. Here, we evaluate differences between forecast performance and computational requirements between daily and weekly COVID-19 incidence data from the nine provinces of South Africa as forecasting inputs. We use the EpiNow2 R package as the core forecasting engine in an analysis pipeline that simulates in situ realtime forecasting with varying data streams.  We evaluate generated forecasts against realized outcomes using the continuous ranked probability score (CRPS) and Effective Sample Size per second as measures of forecast performance and computational efficiency respectively. We find consistent trends in forecast performance (CRPS) and computational efficiency (ESS per second) across time, location, and forecast target resolution. Although both data inputs produced comparable forecast performance, the lower resolution weekly data inputs had lower computational efficiency. We describe a workflow for achieving comparable fits to data between daily and weekly data that can be applicable to similar forecasting problems. The extent to which these tradeoffs matter is context-specific, and varies depending on the public health question at hand. Therefore, the overall analytical costs, including collecting higher temporal resolution data and supplying greater computational resources, need to be weighed against the benefits of improved decision-making outcomes, like more prompt interventions and fewer false alarms. This analysis provides useful evidence towards establishing benchmark analyses for that kind of valuation of forecasting activities.
author-summary: |
  Epidemic forecasters must often decide whether to use detailed daily case reports or coarser weekly totals as model inputs. Daily data are considered the gold standard, but they are costlier to collect and process. We systematically compared forecasts of COVID-19 cases across nine South African provinces using the EpiNow2 modelling framework with daily, weekly, and rescaled weekly data inputs. We evaluated both forecast accuracy (using the Continuous Ranked Probability Score) and computational efficiency (using effective sample size per second and adaptive refit counts). Our results show that daily and weekly data inputs produced comparable forecast performance, but the weekly data required more computational effort to achieve reliable model convergence. The rescaled weekly approach, which compressed weeks into pseudo-days, achieved high sampling efficiency but substantially worse predictive accuracy. These findings provide practical guidance for balancing data collection costs against forecast quality and computational resources, and offer a workflow for achieving comparable fits across temporal resolutions that can be adapted to other forecasting problems.

# Introduction

Infectious disease forecasts are increasingly used to inform public health
decisions such as resource allocation and the timing of interventions during
large outbreaks like influenza [@doms_assessing_2018], Ebola
[@meltzer_modeling_2016; @carias_forecasting_2019], and the COVID-19 pandemic
[@reich_collaborative_2022]. Many approaches for making such forecasts exist,
varying from highly mechanistic, capturing the biological processes, to
statistical, relying on previously observed patterns in the data
[@lauer_infectious_2020; @banholzer_comparison_2023]. However, the conditions
under which a particular forecasting approach is most appropriate remain an open
question [@lauer_infectious_2020].

Infectious disease forecasting models are often calibrated and confronted with
data characterized by noise, incompleteness, and temporal delays in reporting
and the interpretation of forecasts in this context is often of concern
[@reich_collaborative_2022; @nash_realtime_2022; @nash_estimating_2023]. The
temporal resolution of surveillance data is a key determinant of forecast
performance with daily data being the gold standard as data aggregation lowers
data fidelity and may mask short-term fluctuations [@reich_collaborative_2022].
Towards the latter parts of the COVID-19 pandemic, many health agencies shifted
from daily to weekly case reporting to reduce the cost and burden of data
collection [@conway_joint_2024]. Data is often aggregated for several reasons
including removing week-day and weekend reporting biases.

Temporally aggregated data can be used for forecasting, but they also point to
trade-offs between fidelity, bias reduction, and computational burden. Several
recent studies have introduced algorithms to estimate transmission from
aggregated incidence data. The EpiEstim R package uses an
expectation-maximisation method for reconstructing daily case counts from weekly
reports, allowing rapid estimation of time-varying reproduction numbers
[@nash_estimating_2023]. Another approach applied simulation-based methods using
Approximate Bayesian Computation (ABC), recovering reproduction numbers
accurately from weekly data, albeit with increased algorithmic complexity
resulting from the repeated simulation of cases using ABC
[@ogi-gittins_simulation-based_2025]. A Sequential Monte Carlo framework fit to
renewal models either with day-of-week effects or with weekly aggregation has
achieved good performance with lower root-mean-square error and CRPS than a
chosen baseline model [@steyn_primer_2025]. Although these methods demonstrate
that aggregated data can be accommodated, their focus is primarily on
retrospective inference (e.g., estimating reproduction numbers or elimination
probabilities) rather than forecast performance on unseen data. Moreover, there
is little discussion of how computational effort scales with data resolution or
of how to systematically combine diagnostic checks with proper scoring rules to
interpret performance.

The forecasting research community has established several methods for scoring
[@gneiting_strictly_2007; @mitchell_proper_2017; @pic_proper_2024] and
evaluating [@tabataba_framework_2017] forecasts. The choice of score/metric
depends on the forecast type (point, interval, and probabilistic) and ranges
from traditional aggregate measures of distance to Proper Scoring Rules
[@lauer_infectious_2020; @gneiting_strictly_2007; @mitchell_proper_2017; @pic_proper_2024; @bracher_evaluating_2021].
Forecast evaluation metrics such as the continuous ranked probability score
(CRPS) quantify the distance between predicted and observed distributions and
are widely adopted to assess forecast performance against observed data
[@gneiting_strictly_2007; @bracher_evaluating_2021; @funk_assessing_2019].
Recent work highlights that while existing metrics address theoretical concerns
such as calibration and sharpness, they rarely address the operational
challenges of generating forecasts, including reporting frequency and
computational resourcing, pointing to a need for evaluation frameworks that
bridge statistical evaluation and practical relevance [@murphy_what_1993].

Here, we benchmark a method for handling aggregated data in the EpiNow2 R
package version 1.7.1 [@abbott_estimating_2020; @abbott_epinow2_2025]. Briefly,
the EpiNow2 approach models daily latent infections using the renewal equation
and maps them to observations using discrete convolutions of delay
distributions, including the incubation period and reporting delays. We generate
forecasts from daily and weekly COVID-19 reported cases in South Africa between
March 2020 - August 2022 [@marivate_coronavirus_2020; @marivate_use_2020],
evaluate their accuracy using CRPS, assess convergence through rhat
[@vehtari_rank-normalization_2021] and divergent transitions, and computational
efficiency via effective sample size per second. By combining proper scoring
rules with diagnostic measures, we quantify how forecast performance and
computational requirements vary with data granularity and demonstrate how to
achieve comparable fits across temporal resolutions. Our findings provide a
transparent assessment of the trade-offs inherent in using aggregated data for
real-time forecasting and offer practical guidance for balancing data collection
efforts with forecasting needs, thereby advancing the development of evaluation
standards and improving the utility of epidemic forecasts for public health
decision-making.

# Methods

We developed a pipeline (@fig-pipeline-flowchart) to get and clean observed
data, generate forecasts of reported cases, and extract associated computational
quantities such as MCMC convergence metrics and diagnostics and model run times,
score the forecasts, and consolidate the outcomes for analysis and
visualisation. In the following sections, we provide more detail on the
individual parts of the pipeline.

![A schematic of the analysis pipeline. The pipeline consists of four main stages: Data Preparation (getting and cleaning raw provincial daily data, aggregating to weekly, and generating rescaled weekly data), Forecasting Models (daily, weekly, and rescaled weekly models), Evaluation (forecast scoring using CRPS and diagnostics including divergences and ESS tail per second), and Visualisation (plotting log(Incidence) vs log(CRPS) and log(Incidence) vs log(ESS tail/sec) and ratchets).](analysis_pipeline.png){#fig-pipeline-flowchart}

## Data

We obtained and cleaned cumulative COVID-19 case counts for the nine South
African provinces [@marivate_coronavirus_2020; @marivate_use_2020]. The cleaning
process focused on common reporting issues. We removed two all-NA report dates
($2020-03-27$ and $2020-04-07$). We also converted the cumulative counts to
daily incidence per province using time-ordered differencing of non-missing
values. We then corrected three reporting artefacts using a series of steps as
follows:

- When a positive incidence case count had an equal neighbouring negative count
  (or vice versa), both values were set to zero.
- Using the cumulative series, we identified instances where negative daily
  incidence indicated that cumulative counts had been swapped; in these cases,
  we corrected the surrounding three-day window by converting the negative value
  to positive and adjusting the adjacent days so that the cumulative series
  remained strictly increasing.
- For any remaining negative daily values, we redistributed counts between a
  negative count and its positive neighbor by averaging the two values, ensuring
  both became non-negative while preserving the overall total incidence.

After cleaning the time series, we ensured each province had a non-negative
daily time series for downstream aggregation and forecasting.

We aggregated the daily incidence time series into a weekly dataset to represent
the scenario where data is reported on a weekly basis. Weekly observations were
aligned to a fixed reporting weekday (Friday). To preserve this alignment, the
front of each provincial time series was padded with missing values when needed,
and weekly incidence was computed as differences in cumulative incidence between
consecutive Friday reports. From the weekly datasets, we also generated a
rescaled weekly dataset. The rescaled weekly data was a variant of the weekly
data that represented each weekly total as if it occurred on a single day. This
allowed us to evaluate forecasts based on data where all observations were
spaced one week apart while preserving comparability with the other two
datasets.

In addition to province-level datasets, we generated a national (RSA) daily,
weekly, and rescaled weekly time series by summing across provinces and
processed it through the same forecasting and scoring pipelines.

In summary, the three types of data inputs were used to reflect common
observation and reporting patterns:

- daily: both the latent process and the observation process happen on a daily
  time scale
- weekly: the latent process happens on a daily time scale but the reports are
  generated on a weekly time scale
- rescaled weekly: both the latent and observation process happen on a weekly
  time scale

## Forecasting

We used EpiNow2's default model (`epinow()`) to generate 2-week ahead (14 days)
forecasts of COVID-19 reported cases for each of the nine provinces of South
Africa.

We fitted the 10-week chunks of the daily, weekly, and rescaled weekly data
inputs, using 2-week sliding windows, and generated 2-week (14 days) ahead
forecasts for each slide. Before each fit, we removed leading zero-incidence
observations within each sliding window to reduce instability from pre-epidemic
periods. Slides where the training window contained fewer non-zero observations
than twice the forecast horizon (4 weeks or 28 days) were skipped, producing no
forecast for that window. This approach allowed for consistent evaluation across
different phases of the epidemic.

We configured the observation model for each of the three input datasets to
match the different observation patterns. For the daily data, the observation
model accounted for day-of-week reporting effects but this was turned off for
the weekly and rescaled weekly data because the observations already reflect
weekly totals.

EpiNow2 default model models the latent process on a daily scale. For weekly
aggregated data, it accounts for the implicit missing dates and accumulates the
modelled reported cases into weekly forecasts corresponding to the dates in the
observed data. In this work, when we generated forecasts from the weekly
resolution data, we effectively set Saturday through Thursday as missing (NA's),
modelled those missing dates, and accumulated the realised reports to Fridays.
EpiNow2's model, however, does not explicitly model data on the rescaled weekly
scale, so we made a few modifications to the data and parameters to allow for
this use case. We mapped each observed week date to one step on a pseudo-daily
time scale by replacing the weekly dates with consecutive daily dates. Along
with this, we also rescaled the parameter values as described later in this
section. The training window was set to 10 pseudo-days (i.e. 10 weeks) and the
forecast horizon to 2 pseudo-days (i.e. 2 weeks). After fitting, forecast dates
were remapped back to their original calendar-week dates.

The model was parameterised as follows. For the daily and weekly models, the
incubation period was specified as a LogNormal distribution obtained from the
epiparameter database [@linton_incubation_2020; @lambert_epiparameter_2025],
truncated at the 99.9th percentile of the fitted distribution. The generation
time was set to a Gamma distribution with mean 7.12 days, standard deviation
1.72 days, and a maximum of 10 days, based on estimates for the SARS-CoV-2 Alpha
variant [@manica_estimation_2022]. For the rescaled weekly pipeline, the
parameters of the incubation period and generation time were divided by 7.

The reporting delay was specified as a LogNormal distribution with meanlog =
0.58 and sdlog = 0.47 (corresponding to approximately mean 2 days, standard
deviation 1 day), truncated at a maximum of 10 days. The prior on the
time-varying reproduction number $R_t$ was set to LogNormal(meanlog = 0.69,
sdlog = 0.05), corresponding to an approximate mean of 2 and standard deviation
of 0.1.

EpiNow2 uses Stan for model fitting and provides the option to use either the
`cmdstanr` R package [@cmdstanr] or `rstan` R package [@rstan] as the backend.
We used the former where available, running $4$ chains in parallel with $4$
cores and returning $5,000$ total posterior samples across all chains, with an
initial step size of $0.1$.

When fitting to the data in a sliding window, we allowed the model to be
refitted (ratchets) until reasonable MCMC convergence and Stan diagnostic
criteria, defined below, were achieved. For each ratchet, we tuned Stan's
adapt-delta parameter to ensure efficient sampling and reliable convergence.
Following recommendations from members of the Stan Community
[@betancourt_identity_2020], the adapt-delta parameter was initiated at $0.80$
and increased by $25/%$ until it reached $0.99$, which is the upper limit in
Stan. Based on the number of refits needed to go from adapt-delta of $0.8$ to
$0.99$ in these increments, we determined that each slide could be refitted a
maximum of $11$ times. At each refit, we continued only when at most two of
three diagnostic criteria were met (divergences, $\hat{R}$, and bulk ESS). When
the ratchet limit was reached, we returned the last model output irrespective of
the diagnostic measurements.

We measured convergence using three metrics. The bulk effective sample size
(ESS) quantifies how many independent draws contain the same amount of
information as the dependent sample obtained by the MCMC algorithm
[@vehtari_rank-normalization_2021; @stan_development_team_stan_2025; @betancourt_conceptual_2018].
We limited bulk ESS to at least 100 per chain, hence a minimum of 400 for the 4
chains, based on recommendations with higher values of ESS indicating efficient
mixing of the chains [@vehtari_rank-normalization_2021]. We additionally tracked
$\hat{R}$, which is a measure of MCMC convergence and limited it to below $1.01$
[@vehtari_rank-normalization_2021]. The number of divergent transitions during
sampling, which indicates that the Hamiltonian Monte Carlo sampler has failed to
accurately explore the posterior distribution due to irregular or complex
geometry, potentially leading to biased inference, was limited to below 0.25% of
the total posterior draws across all four chains (approximately 13 divergent
transitions when obtaining $5,000$ posterior draws in total across chains)
[@stan_development_team_stan_2025; @betancourt_conceptual_2018; @mcelreath_statistical_2018].
We also tracked the model run times for computing efficiency metrics like the
bulk ESS per second.

The diagnostic results were summarised per province and dataset type, and time
series of the bulk ESS per second and number of ratchets were plotted alongside
reported cases to visualise sampling efficiency over time.

We saved outputs of forecast reported case counts per slide, MCMC diagnostics
(including divergences, $\hat{R}$, and basic/bulk/tail ESS), and model run
times.

## Forecast scoring and evaluation

We evaluated forecast accuracy using the Continuous Ranked Probability Score
(CRPS) given by

$$
CRPS(F, x) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} (F(y) - 1\{y \geq x \})^2 dy
$$

Where $F(\Theta)$ is the cumulative distribution function of $\Theta$, here,
referring to the observed values, $x$, and forecast values, $y$, and 1 is the
indicator function
[@gneiting_strictly_2007; @bracher_evaluating_2021; @bosse_scoring_2023]. The
CRPS is a proper scoring rule that quantifies the distance between the
cumulative distribution of the forecast values and the observed case counts. The
lower the CRPS value, the better. Forecasts were scored in five combinations
within each slide:

- Daily forecast vs. daily observations -- daily forecasts compared with daily
  reported cases.
- Daily forecast vs. weekly observations -- daily forecasts aggregated to weekly
  totals and compared to weekly data.
- Weekly forecast vs. daily observations -- weekly forecasts disaggregated on a
  daily scale and compared to the daily series.
- Weekly forecast vs. weekly observations -- weekly forecasts compared to weekly
  observations.
- Rescaled weekly forecast vs. weekly observations -- rescaled weekly forecasts
  compared to weekly observations.

When forecasts and observations were on different temporal resolutions,
predictions were accumulated between observed report dates before scoring so
that CRPS was evaluated on aligned observation times. Specifically, forecast
samples were joined to the observation dates, cumulative sums were computed
within each sample and slide, and the accumulated predictions were then
differenced at the observed time points to obtain aligned forecast values.

We compared the default model's performance across the daily, weekly, and
rescaled weekly data inputs using CRPS and ESS per second. For computational
efficiency visualisation, we used tail ESS per second, computed as tail ESS for
a slide divided by elapsed fitting time in seconds, where elapsed fitting time
was defined as the maximum across chains of the combined warmup and sampling
time, summed over all ratchets within a slide. The two metrics represented
forecast quality and computational efficiency respectively. Forecast scoring was
facilitated by the scoringutils R package [@bosse_evaluating_2024].

We plotted a time series of the CRPS and ESS/sec alongside the time series of
log-transformed daily and weekly cases for easy interpretability. We also pooled
together the results across time and computed the geometric mean of the CRPS
ratio relative to the model using daily data, calculated as the exponentiated
mean of the log-ratios and stratified by province, forecast type, and evaluation
resolution. To provide more details of model computational requirements, we also
showed a time series of the number of refits per slide per province and for all
three input types.

## Data and code availability

The analysis used COVID-19 data from South Africa. The code for the analysis is
available at https://github.com/epiforecasts/daily-vs-weekly-forecast-eval.

All analyses were done with R version 4.5.1 [@r_core_team_r_2025] and
orchestrated with GNU make [@noauthor_gnu_2006]. The SARS-CoV-2 incubation
period was obtained from the epiparameter R package v0.4.1.900
[@lambert_epiparameter_2025], which stores a database of literature parameter
estimates.

# Results

We present province-level results using the Eastern Cape (EC) as a
representative example; equivalent figures for all other provinces are provided
in the Supplementary Materials. The patterns described below were consistent
across all nine provinces and the national aggregate (RSA).

## Forecast performance

@fig-panel-scores-EC shows the CRPS time series for the EC alongside the
observed daily and weekly incidence. On a log scale, CRPS tracks the incidence
level closely: scores rise by one to two orders of magnitude during epidemic
wave peaks and fall during inter-wave troughs, reflecting the larger absolute
errors inherent to higher case counts. When evaluated against daily
observations, forecasts trained on daily and weekly data produce comparable CRPS
values, with the daily-trained model performing slightly better during periods
of rapidly changing incidence. When evaluated against weekly observations, the
daily-trained and weekly-trained forecasts again show similar accuracy. In
contrast, the rescaled weekly forecasts exhibit substantially worse CRPS ---
approximately one to two orders of magnitude higher than the other two
approaches --- across both evaluation resolutions, indicating that the
time-compression strategy degrades predictive performance.

![Forecast performance for the Eastern Cape province (EC). The top panel shows the daily (black points) and weekly (red horizontal segments) COVID-19 incidence. The bottom panel displays the Continuous Ranked Probability Score (CRPS) for daily, weekly, and rescaled weekly forecast targets (colours), with both incidence and CRPS shown on a log10 scale. The rows in the bottom panel are faceted by the temporal resolution of the evaluation data (daily or weekly). Equivalent plots for all other provinces are provided in the Supplementary Materials.](../local/figures/fig_panel_scores_EC.png){#fig-panel-scores-EC}

## Computational diagnostics

@fig-panel-diagnostics-EC displays the tail ESS per second and the number of
adaptive ratchets for the EC. The rescaled weekly model achieves the highest
sampling efficiency, with tail ESS per second typically in the range of 1--10,
reflecting the smaller effective dataset size in the compressed time
representation. The daily model yields intermediate efficiency at approximately
0.1--0.3 ESS per second, while the weekly model has the lowest efficiency at
roughly 0.01--0.1 ESS per second. The ratchet counts mirror this pattern in
reverse: the weekly model consistently requires the most adaptive refits,
typically 5--12 per slide, indicating that convergence is most difficult for the
weekly data configuration. The daily model requires the fewest ratchets, usually
0--2 per slide, while the rescaled weekly model falls in between with variable
ratchet counts. These patterns were consistent across all nine provinces and the
national aggregate.

![Computational diagnostics for the Eastern Cape province (EC). The top panel shows the daily and weekly COVID-19 incidence. The middle panel displays the tail Effective Sample Size (ESS) per second on a log10 scale, representing sampling efficiency for different forecast targets (colours). The bottom panel shows the number of model ratchets (adaptive refits) required to achieve convergence for each forecast slide. Equivalent results for all other provinces are available in the Supplementary Materials.](../local/figures/fig_panel_diagnostics_EC.png){#fig-panel-diagnostics-EC}

## Relative performance across provinces

@fig-crps-all-provs-summarised compares the geometric mean CRPS ratio relative
to the daily-trained baseline across all provinces. When evaluated against daily
observations, the weekly-trained model produces CRPS approximately 1.5--3 times
higher than the daily-trained baseline, with the majority of provinces clustered
between 1.5× and 2.5×. When evaluated against weekly observations, the
weekly-trained model achieves CRPS ratios close to or slightly below 1,
indicating comparable or marginally better performance than the daily-trained
model at the weekly resolution. The rescaled weekly model performs markedly
worse, with CRPS ratios of approximately 30--60 times higher than the
daily-trained baseline when both are evaluated against weekly observations.
Province-to-province variability within each comparison scenario is small
relative to the differences between scenarios, indicating that the relative
performance of each approach is robust across locations. The national aggregate
(RSA) falls near the centre of the provincial distribution in all three
scenarios.

![Relative forecast performance across all nine South African provinces and the national total (RSA). The plot shows the geometric mean of the Continuous Ranked Probability Score (CRPS) relative to the baseline model trained on daily data. Comparisons are shown for three scenarios: weekly aggregated training data tested against daily observations, rescaled weekly training tested against weekly observations, and weekly aggregated training tested against weekly observations. Values above the dashed line ($y=1$) indicate worse performance than the daily-trained baseline, while values below indicate better performance. Provinces are ordered by population size and colour-coded, with the national total (RSA) included for comparison.](../local/figures/fig_crps_summary_all_provs.png){#fig-crps-all-provs-summarised}

# Discussion

This study highlights the trade-offs of temporal aggregation in epidemiological
forecasting. Daily data offer greater accuracy for short-term predictions,
albeit at higher computational costs and diagnostic instability. Weekly data
provide computational efficiency and smoother trends but sacrifice granularity
and responsiveness to rapid changes in case dynamics. Though we did not
explicitly investigate this element, it stands to reason that the underlying
surveillance system to support higher frequency reporting would also entail
additional cost (e.g. more required storage space, more bandwidth to support
more frequent access).

Our central finding on forecast performance is that daily and weekly data inputs
yield comparable CRPS when forecasts are evaluated at the same temporal
resolution. When evaluated against weekly observations, the weekly-trained model
matches or slightly outperforms the daily-trained model (geometric mean CRPS
ratio near 1×), and even when evaluated against daily observations the
weekly-trained model is only 1.5--3 times worse. In contrast, the rescaled
weekly approach produces CRPS 30--60 times larger than the daily-trained
baseline. This pronounced degradation likely arises because compressing weekly
intervals into pseudo-daily steps distorts the temporal dynamics that EpiNow2's
renewal equation is designed to capture: generation times, incubation periods,
and reporting delays are all divided by seven, fundamentally altering the
relationship between latent infections and observed cases. EpiNow2's built-in
`fill_missing()` mechanism, which explicitly models the accumulation of reports
across days within a week, preserves these epidemiological relationships and
explains why the standard weekly approach remains competitive with daily
forecasting.

The computational requirements of the three approaches present a striking
counterpoint to their predictive performance. The weekly model, despite
producing forecast accuracy comparable to the daily model, required
substantially more computational effort: it consistently needed the most
adaptive refits (typically 5--12 ratchets per slide versus 0--2 for the daily
model) and exhibited the lowest sampling efficiency (approximately 0.01--0.1
tail ESS per second, compared with 0.1--0.3 for daily). This additional
computational burden reflects the challenge of fitting a model designed for
daily latent dynamics to data observed only once per week, where the posterior
geometry becomes more complex due to the implicit marginalisation over
unobserved daily counts. Conversely, the rescaled weekly model achieved the
highest sampling efficiency (1--10 tail ESS per second) because its compressed
time axis reduced the effective number of latent time steps, simplifying the
posterior. However, this computational efficiency came at the cost of
dramatically worse predictive performance, demonstrating that sampling
efficiency and forecast quality are not interchangeable objectives.

These results have two stakeholders. To the users of EpiNow2, it addressed
questions of how EpiNow2 performs under degrading data resolution conditions and
the computational requirements to achieve reasonable model fits. To the tool
developers, these results inform ways to improve the underlying model to tackle
the issue of degrading data conditions.

The findings emphasize the importance of aligning forecast resolution with the
specific objectives of a public health response. For example, aggregated data
may be suitable for long-term trend analysis, while high-resolution daily data
are better for rapid outbreak detection and intervention planning.

Several limitations should be considered when interpreting these results. First,
we used a single forecasting framework (EpiNow2), and our findings may not
generalise to other modelling approaches that handle temporal aggregation
differently. Second, we focused on a single disease (COVID-19) in a single
country (South Africa), and the relative performance of daily versus weekly
inputs may vary for pathogens with different generation times or in settings
with different surveillance characteristics. Third, the rescaled weekly pipeline
used a hardcoded incubation period (LogNormal with mean 5/7 and sd 1/7) that
approximates but may not exactly replicate the distribution obtained from the
epiparameter database at runtime, introducing a minor inconsistency between the
rescaled and standard pipelines. Finally, the analysis relies on reported case
data that are subject to surveillance artefacts including reporting delays,
retrospective corrections, and negative incidence values arising from cumulative
count adjustments, all of which were addressed through data cleaning but may
still influence forecast performance.

Our findings complement and extend prior work on temporal aggregation in
epidemiological inference. @nash_estimating_2023 demonstrated that daily
reproduction numbers can be recovered from weekly data using
expectation-maximisation within EpiEstim, while
@ogi-gittins_simulation-based_2025 showed that ABC-based methods can accurately
estimate reproduction numbers from aggregated counts, albeit with greater
algorithmic complexity. @steyn_primer_2025 applied Sequential Monte Carlo
methods to renewal models with weekly aggregation and achieved competitive
performance relative to models with day-of-week effects. These studies focused
primarily on retrospective inference --- estimating reproduction numbers or
elimination probabilities --- rather than on evaluating the quality of
out-of-sample forecasts. Our work extends this literature in two respects: we
systematically compare forecast performance on unseen data across daily, weekly,
and rescaled weekly inputs using proper scoring rules (CRPS), and we jointly
assess computational diagnostics (ESS per second, ratchet counts, divergences)
alongside forecast accuracy, providing a more complete picture of the practical
trade-offs involved in using temporally aggregated data.

The evaluation of scoring methodologies and diagnostics in this study also
provides a framework for future analyses. Metrics such as CRPS, effective sample
sizes, and divergence rates offer robust measures of forecast reliability and
can be adapted to various modeling contexts. Though the daily data did generally
provide better forecast performance, the algorithmic extensions to explicitly
account for missingness kept the weekly resolution approach competitive. Such
model enhancements may not always be practical, but this work suggests they can
be valuable.

For practitioners deciding between daily and weekly data inputs, we recommend
the following workflow. First, if daily data are available and computational
resources permit, daily-resolution forecasting with EpiNow2 provides the best
combination of forecast accuracy and sampling efficiency. Second, when only
weekly data are available --- or when daily collection and processing costs are
prohibitive --- the standard weekly approach using EpiNow2's `fill_missing()`
mechanism can achieve comparable forecast accuracy, provided that sufficient
computational budget is allocated for adaptive tuning; practitioners should
expect approximately 5--12 adaptive refits per forecast window and should
monitor convergence using the diagnostic thresholds described in this study
(divergences below 0.25% of total draws, $\hat{R}$ below 1.01, and bulk ESS
above 400). Third, the rescaled weekly approach, while computationally
efficient, should be avoided for operational forecasting given its substantially
degraded predictive performance. More broadly, we recommend that forecast
evaluation routinely combine proper scoring rules with computational
diagnostics, as our results demonstrate that high sampling efficiency does not
guarantee good forecast quality, and adequate convergence diagnostics are
necessary to ensure that model outputs are reliable for decision-making.
